title: Random Reed-Solomon Codes and Random Linear Codes are Locally Equivalent
authors: Matan Levi (Ben-Gurion University, Israel), Jonathan Mosheiff (Ben-Gurion University, Israel), Nikhil Shagrithaya (University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA)
abstract: We establish an equivalence between two important random ensembles of linear codes: random linear codes (RLCs) and random Reed-Solomon (RS) codes. Specifically, we show that these models exhibit identical behavior with respect to key combinatorial properties---such as list-decodability and list-recoverability---when the alphabet size is sufficiently large. We introduce monotone-decreasing local coordinate-wise linear (LCL) properties, a new class of properties tailored for the large alphabet regime. This class encompasses list-decodability, list-recoverability, and their average-weight variants. We develop a framework for analyzing these properties and prove a threshold theorem for RLCs: for any LCL property P, there exists a threshold rate RPRP? such that RLCs are likely to satisfy P when R<R_P and unlikely to do so when R>R_P?. We extend this threshold theorem to random RS codes and show that they share the same threshold RPRP?, thereby establishing the equivalence between the two ensembles and enabling a unified analysis of list-recoverability and related properties. Applying our framework, we compute the threshold rate for list-decodability, proving that both random RS codes and RLCs achieve the generalized Singleton bound. This recovers a recent result of Alrabiah, Guruswami, and Li (2023) via elementary methods. Additionally, we prove an upper bound on the list-recoverability threshold and conjecture that this bound is tight. Our approach suggests a plausible pathway for proving this conjecture and thereby pinpointing the list-recoverability parameters of both models. Indeed, following the release of a prior version of this paper, Li and Shagrithaya (2025) used our equivalence theorem to show that random RS codes are near-optimally list-recoverable.

Abstract—We establish an equivalence between two important random ensembles of linear codes: random linear
codes (RLCs) and random Reed-Solomon (RS) codes.
Specifically, we show that these models exhibit identical
behavior with respect to key combinatorial properties—
such as list-decodability and list-recoverability—when the
alphabet size is sufficiently large.
We introduce monotone-decreasing local coordinate-wise
linear (LCL) properties, a new class of properties tailored
for the large alphabet regime. This class encompasses listdecodability, list-recoverability, and their average-weight
variants. We develop a framework for analyzing these
properties and prove a threshold theorem for RLCs: for
any LCL property P, there exists a threshold rate RP
such that RLCs are likely to satisfy P when R < RP and
unlikely to do so when R > RP . We extend this threshold
theorem to random RS codes and show that they share the
same threshold RP , thereby establishing the equivalence
between the two ensembles and enabling a unified analysis
of list-recoverability and related properties.
Applying our framework, we compute the threshold
rate for list-decodability, proving that both random RS
codes and RLCs achieve the generalized Singleton bound.
This recovers a recent result of Alrabiah, Guruswami,
and Li (2023) via elementary methods. Additionally, we
prove an upper bound on the list-recoverability threshold
and conjecture that this bound is tight. Our approach
suggests a plausible pathway for proving this conjecture
and thereby pinpointing the list-recoverability parameters
of both models. Indeed, following the release of a prior
version of this paper, Li and Shagrithaya (2025) used our
equivalence theorem to show that random RS codes are
near-optimally list-recoverable.

B. Local Code Properties and the LCL Framework
Our notion of LCL properties extends a general framework, initially introduced in [MRRSW20], for studying list-decodability and list-recoverability as part of a
broader class of code properties. A set of words in Fnq
that all lie within the same Hamming ball of radius ρn is
called ρ-clustered. A set of words X ⊆ Fnq is said to be
(ρ, ℓ) -recovery-clustered if there exists a sequence of
sets Z1 , . . . , Zn ⊆ Fq , each of size at most ℓ, such that
for every x ∈ X, the condition |{i ∈ [n] | xi ∈
/ Zi }| ≤
ρn holds. Thus, a code C is (ρ, L) -list-decodable (or
(ρ, ℓ, L) -list-recoverable) if and only if it does not
contain a ρ-clustered (or (ρ, ℓ) -recovery-clustered) set
of size L + 1. We interpret a clustered (or recoveryclustered) set of codewords in C as a witness to the
code’s non-list-decodability (or non-list-recoverability).
This leads to the observation that list-decodability and
list-recoverability have short witnesses, drawing a natural
analogy to CO -NP languages or Π1 logical formulas.
In [MRRSW20], this viewpoint was used to study
list-decodability and list-recoverability within a newly
defined class of (monotone-decreasing) local code
properties. A property is said to be local if it has
short witnesses, like clustered sets for list-decodability.
The main finding of [MRRSW20] is that Gallagher
codes, a random ensemble of LDPC codes, possess
local properties similar to those of RLCs, meaning they
are just as list-decodable and list-recoverable (with high
probability). Later, [GM22] extended this framework to
show that randomly punctured low-bias codes also
share local properties with RLCs. These results can be
seen as reductions between code ensembles.5
The reduction results in [MRRSW20] and [GM22]
stem from the threshold theorem for local properties
for RLCs [MRRSW20, Theorem 2.8]. This theorem
states that for any local property P, there is a threshold
rate RP such that RLCs with a rate below RP are
likely to satisfy P, whereas those with a rate above RP
are unlikely to do so. An analogous theorem for plain
random codes is proven in [GMRSW22].
The threshold theorem crucially relies on the property
P having short witnesses. For instance, if P is the
property of (ρ, L)-list-decodability, the witnesses are
ρ-clustered sets of size L + 1. To apply the theorem,
subsets of Fbq (where b = L + 1) are classified into
types, and the theorem uses the expected number of

Informally, a property P is b-LCL if it is witnessed
by a small set of codewords x1 , . . . , xb ∈ Fnq such that,
for each 1 ≤ i ≤ n, the vector (x1i , . . . , xbi ) satisfies
certain linear constraints. For example, ρ-clusteredness is
characterized by a large number of equality constraints
(which are, in particular, linear) among x1i , . . . , xbi for
many coordinates 1 ≤ i ≤ n. We provide a formal
treatment in Section II-C.
As mentioned, the LCL framework encompasses listdecodability and list-recoverability, along with their
average-weight variants. It also naturally captures other
properties, such as average pairwise distance (defined in
[CGV13]) and list-decodability from burst errors (e.g.,
[RV09]) under a unified lens.

Another challenge arises in the small q regime, such
as when q = poly(ℓ). Our current methods cannot
directly address list-recoverability in this setting due to
the exponential dependence of q on locality. Relaxing

Furthermore, extending our framework to analyze
highly non-local properties would be valuable. Consider
the following example: fix a large q and let 0 < R < 1,
q (1−R) < ℓ < q, and ε > 0. Let P represent the
property of (0, ℓ, L)-list-recoverability for codes in Fnq ,
where L = ℓn · q −(1−R)n · (1 + ε). Note that P is not a
local property, since L is typically exponential in n, but

Notice that ℓn ·q −(1−R)n is the expected size of the set
C ∩ Z1 × Z2 × · · · × Zn , where C ⊆ Fnq is a fixed code of

P if its maximum intersection with any product set Z1 ×

From a pseudorandomness perspective, a code satisfying

satisfies this property. In particular, do RLCs satisfy

affirmative by [MPSW21] when R > 12 and q is a large
prime. For R ≤ 12 , these questions remain open. We
conjecture that the answer is again positive, provided

Conjecture I.1 (Optimality of RLCs and random RS
codes for LCL properties). For every ε > 0 and b ∈ N,
there exist constants n0 and q0 such that the following
holds: Let P be a b-local (monotone-decreasing) LCL

agreement constraints. The concept of a b-local profile extends this framework by encoding constraints on
coordinates in a more general manner, permitting the
representation of linear constraints rather than merely
agreement constraints. This generalization plays a crucial
role in establishing the threshold theorem for RLCs and
in demonstrating the equivalence between RLCs and
random RS codes.
